messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 66
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Roofer
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 36

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Olfactory (Smell): Related smells
  Maladaptive Strategies: Past Dwelling: I dwell on how I used to be before the event, Avoid Assertiveness: never disagree or assert myself to avoid conflict, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
  Memory: Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Hopelessness: I have no future, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Clinical Vignette: Thuan

Thuan was fifty-eight when the accident happened on a commercial roofing job in suburban Atlanta. He had been working in residential and commercial roofing for nearly thirty years—meticulous work that required precision and an almost meditative focus on the task at hand. That afternoon, he and a younger colleague were applying a sealant to the flat roof of a three-story office building. The product had been delivered in unmarked containers; the site supervisor assured them it was standard, approved, nothing to worry about. Within minutes of opening the first container, Thuan felt a burning sensation in his throat and sinuses. The smell was acrid, chemical, nothing like the familiar odors he had encountered across three decades in the trade. His colleague noticed it too, but by then both men were already inhaling the fumes. Thuan remembered the panic—the sudden awareness that something was profoundly wrong, that the air itself had become hostile. He stumbled toward the roof's edge, gasping, his vision blurring. Emergency services arrived within twenty minutes. The substance turned out to be an industrial-grade solvent that had been improperly labeled and stored; it contained compounds that caused acute chemical pneumonitis. Thuan spent four days in the hospital, where doctors confirmed that his lungs had been exposed to toxic levels of volatile organic compounds. He was discharged with a prescription for corticosteroids and an inhaler, told that his respiratory function would likely recover fully, though it might take months.

Eight years have passed since that day. Thuan is now sixty-six, and he has not returned to roofing. The physical recovery was complete—his pulmonary function tests normalized within a year—but something else did not heal. He came to believe that he could no longer trust his own judgment about safety, that he had failed to notice or prevent something catastrophic that nearly killed him. The world, in his mind, had become saturated with invisible dangers. What frightened him most was the thought that he might miss another warning sign, that the next threat could come from anywhere, disguised as something ordinary. He had come to believe he had no future worth planning for—that his body had been fundamentally compromised, that his capacity to work and contribute had been stolen from him.

When darkness falls, Thuan's vigilance intensifies. He lies awake beside his wife, Mei, listening to the house settle, unable to relax even in the safety of their bedroom. Waking in the dark triggers an immediate surge of dread; his heart accelerates, and his mind floods with the sensory memory of that afternoon—the burning in his throat, the chemical taste, the feeling of his lungs closing. The memory plays like a film he cannot stop: the moment he opened the container, the smell hitting him, the blur of panic, the ambulance. The images are vivid and intrusive, accompanied by the full emotional intensity of the original terror, sometimes arriving without any visual component at all, just a crushing wave of fear and suffocation. These nocturnal episodes have become so routine that Thuan now dreads bedtime. He tries hard not to think about what happened, pushing the memories away during the day, but at night his effort collapses. The suppression leaves him exhausted and hypervigilant by morning.

The smell of antiseptic—in hospitals, in some cleaning products, even in the waiting rooms of doctors' offices—transports him instantly back to those four hospital days and the chemical exposure that preceded them. When Mei needed a routine colonoscopy last year, Thuan accompanied her to the outpatient surgery center. The moment they entered the corridor and he caught the familiar sharp scent of disinfectant, his breathing became shallow, his concentration fractured. He could not focus on Mei's reassurances or the nurse's explanations. The threat felt immediate and inescapable. He sat in the waiting area gripping the armrest, unable to relax, certain that the air itself was contaminated. He left the building and waited in the car, avoiding the space entirely, unable to assess whether it was truly safe. This pattern has repeated itself: he avoids hospitals, avoids unfamiliar places where he cannot quickly identify exits or assess potential chemical hazards, avoids anything that might expose him to similar smells.

His avoidance has reshaped his life in ways both obvious and subtle. He stopped asserting himself with Mei, never disagreeing with her plans or expressing his own needs, believing that conflict might destabilize the fragile equilibrium he has constructed. He dwells constantly on how he used to be—the confident craftsman, the man who could read a roof and know exactly what it needed, the man who trusted himself. That version of him feels irretrievable. His inability to relax, his difficulty concentrating, his conviction that he cannot rely on himself—these thoughts reinforce his belief that the world is fundamentally dangerous and that he is powerless within it. Because he believes the world is dangerous and that he cannot trust his own judgment, he finds himself hypervigilant to any potential threat, scanning for smells, for darkness, for unfamiliar situations. This vigilance keeps him trapped in a state of perpetual threat detection, which in turn triggers the memories and the sense of helplessness that feeds his conviction that he has no future.

Mei finally insisted he see someone after she found him one morning at 3 a.m. sitting on the back porch in the dark, unable to return to bed, unable to explain why he was so afraid. She told him that he was disappearing, that the man she married was being consumed by something he could not name. It is this—the fear that he is becoming unrecognizable even to himself, that his life has shrunk to the size of a prison he has built from his own terror—that has finally brought Thuan to seek help.
